svg.text: Diffraction, beats and the intensity of a wave

g.text: bending of waves round edges and through openings near
the wavelength in size; longer wavelength, more spreading
two waves of slightly different frequency travelling the same way give a periodic rise and fall of
loudness: beats; number of beats per second = fA - fB = 32 - 28 = 4; hard to hear above 10 Hz
beat frequency f_beat = 1/T, T = time between successive loud sounds; tune a string against a
note of known frequency until no beats are heard (guitar, piano, violin, drums, flute, organ)
Example 7.7: 256 Hz fork, 3 beats; waxing it gives 1 beat, so the second fork is 253 Hz,
not 259 Hz (that would give more beats); tuning forks were invented by F. J. Shore in 1711
intensity = energy per unit area per unit time
in the direction of propagation, in W m^-2
k depends on the wave and the medium; amplitude
and frequency are independent (volume, not pitch)
Example 7.8: I = 0.5 W m^-2 at 3.0 m: P = I x 4 pi r^2
Example 7.9: 50 W over 314 m^2: I = 0.159 W m^-2

svg.text: progressive waves (water, sound, light) carry energy forward; sound cannot cross a vacuum

g.text: ripple tank: a vibrator makes circular or plane water waves;
a lamp projects the pattern onto a white screen below; blocks
form gaps of different widths to compare the diffraction
Example 7.6: 500 pulses in 10 s: T = 10/500 = 1/50 s, f = 50 Hz
diffraction examples: sound heard round corners and through doors;
X-rays diffracted by crystals (atom spacing near X-ray wavelength);
white light spread into colours by a grating or a CD (0.5 um rulings)
longitudinal (sound): compressions and rarefactions; transverse
(light): crests and troughs; both have wavelength and amplitude
